q: A readiness probe on one pod fails 3 times in a row. What does Kubernetes do?
options: It removes the pod from the Service's list and does not restart it
It restarts the container, then puts the pod back in the Service's list
It deletes the pod, and the Deployment makes a new one with a new name
It rolls back the whole Deployment to the version before
why: Readiness decides who gets traffic. A failed readiness probe only removes the pod from the Service's list. The container keeps running, the kubelet keeps asking, and the pod rejoins when a check passes. Only a failed liveness or startup probe restarts the container.

q: Your app needs 60 seconds to start. Liveness checks every 10 seconds and allows 3 failures, and there is no startup probe. The pod keeps restarting. What do you add?
options: A readiness probe with a longer period
A startup probe with a high failureThreshold
A CPU limit, so the app starts more calmly
A second liveness probe that also checks the database
why: Liveness kills the container after about 30 seconds, before it is up, and the loop repeats. A startup probe (for example 24 failures every 5 seconds, so 120 seconds) holds back liveness and readiness until it passes. After that, liveness takes over.

q: What is the difference between a request and a limit?
options: A request is the ceiling the kernel enforces. A limit is what the scheduler reserves.
They are the same number. Kubernetes only reads one of them.
A request is what the scheduler reserves. A limit is the ceiling the kernel enforces.
A request is for memory only. A limit is for CPU only.
why: The scheduler adds up requests to find a machine with room. The kubelet and the Linux kernel enforce limits. Docker's --memory and --cpus set the same kernel limits.

q: One container goes over its memory limit. Another goes over its CPU limit. What happens?
options: Both are killed by the kernel with exit code 137
Both are throttled: slower, with no error
Memory: throttled and slower. CPU: killed with exit code 137
Memory: killed (OOMKilled, exit 137). CPU: throttled, slower, no error.
why: Over the memory limit the kernel kills the container. In my Docker run it ended with OOMKilled=true and exit code 137. Over the CPU limit the kernel makes it wait: a job that needs 1000 ms took 1960 ms with a limit of 0.5, and nothing failed.

q: A Deployment has 3 replicas, maxSurge 1 and maxUnavailable 0. During a rolling update, what is the most pods that exist and the fewest that are ready?
options: At most 4 exist, and at least 3 are ready
At most 3 exist, and at least 2 are ready
At most 4 exist, and at least 2 are ready
At most 6 exist, and at least 3 are ready
why: maxSurge 1 allows one extra pod, so 3 + 1 = 4 at most. maxUnavailable 0 means all 3 wanted pods must stay ready, so 3 - 0 = 3 at least. Kubernetes starts a new pod, waits for ready, and only then removes an old one.

q: The new version never passes its readiness probe, and the rollout is stuck for 10 minutes. What happens?
options: Kubernetes rolls back to the old version by itself after the deadline
The old pods keep serving. Kubernetes only reports it, and you run kubectl rollout undo.
The new pods get traffic anyway once the deadline passes
All old pods are removed so that the new version can start
why: With maxUnavailable 0, no old pod is removed while the new pod is not ready. The Deployment docs say Kubernetes takes no action on a stalled Deployment other than to report a status condition, and kubectl rollout status ends with an error. With no readiness probe the new pods would count as ready at once and the bug would go live.
